SUPPORT OF PARENTS BY AN ADULT CHILD (FAMILY CODE SECTIONS 4400-4414) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Rowan Avery Ellison · Marguerite Ellison

PARTIES, SCOPE, AND PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Support of Parents Information Sheet concerns Rowan Avery Ellison, an adult child, and Marguerite Ellison, a parent, in connection with a proceeding pending, or that may be filed, in the California superior court for Fresno County. It surveys what California's Family Code Part 4 of Division 9 (“Support of Parents,” sections 4400 through 4414) says about the duty of an adult child to support a parent in need, the related misdemeanor provision in the Penal Code, the public-benefits provision that displaces the duty for certain aid recipients, and the petition procedure by which an adult child may ask a court for relief from the duty on the ground that the parent abandoned the child. It states what the statutes say and what published California opinions have held about them. It does not determine whether Marguerite Ellison is “in need and unable to self-maintain by work” within the meaning of the statute, whether Rowan Avery Ellison has any duty or any defense, what amount (if any) a court would order, or what any party should do; those are matters for a court, or for the parties' own agreement.

THE CORE DUTY — FAMILY CODE SECTIONS 4400, 4401, AND 4402
California is among the states that impose a statutory support duty running from an adult child to a parent. Family Code section 4400 states the duty in a single sentence: an adult child shall, to the extent of the adult child's ability, support a parent who is in need and unable to self-maintain by work — subject to an express opening qualifier, “Except as otherwise provided by law.” Section 4401 makes an adult child's promise to pay for necessaries already furnished to such a parent binding, which supplies a contractual route distinct from a court-ordered support obligation. Section 4402 states that the duty created by this Part is cumulative and not a substitute for any other duty, so its existence does not by itself displace obligations arising elsewhere in California law.

NO COMMON LAW DUTY — DUFFY V. YORDI (1906)
The California Supreme Court held more than a century ago that no duty of a child to support a parent existed at common law, that any such obligation rests entirely on statute, and that the procedure the statute provides for enforcement must be followed. The same opinion described the main purpose of such statutes as protecting the public from the burden of supporting poor people who have children able to support them. Duffy construed former Civil Code section 206, the predecessor from which Family Code sections 4400 and 4401 were later drawn, and its statement of the statutory-origin principle continues to be cited in later California opinions.

HOW THE CALIFORNIA SUPREME COURT HAS DESCRIBED THE DUTY — PEOPLE V. HEITZMAN (1994)
In a 1994 decision addressing the elder-abuse statute, the California Supreme Court described the duty of adult children to support needy parents as deeply rooted in California's statutory law and restated the settled account of its purpose — protecting the public from the burden of supporting people who have children able to support them. The same opinion records the statutory lineage: Family Code section 4400 restates, without substantive change, the first sentence of former Civil Code section 206 and former Civil Code section 242. Heitzman also declined to import the financial-support statutes into the felony elder-abuse statute as the source of a criminal duty to act, reasoning that the legislative purposes of the two bodies of law are materially different.

WHO MAY BRING THE ACTION, AND THE COUNTY’S ROLE — FAMILY CODE SECTION 4403
Section 4403 identifies who may sue. A parent may bring an action against the child to enforce the duty, and a county may bring that action on the parent's behalf. If a county has furnished support to a parent, the statute gives the county the same right the parent had, both to secure reimbursement for what it furnished and to obtain continuing support. The county's right to proceed or to obtain reimbursement is expressly made subject to any limitation otherwise imposed by California law — a qualifier that connects this section to the public-benefits provision discussed elsewhere in this document. Subdivision (c) authorizes the court to order the child to pay the county reasonable attorney's fees and court costs in a county-brought proceeding; the statute states no reciprocal fee provision running the other way.

SETTING THE AMOUNT, AND CONTINUING JURISDICTION — FAMILY CODE SECTIONS 4404 AND 4405
Unlike child support, parent support under this Part has no statewide arithmetic guideline. Section 4404 instead directs the court to consider an enumerated list of circumstances of each party: earning capacity and needs; obligations and assets; age and health; standard of living; and other factors the court deems just and equitable. The final catch-all leaves the weighing to judicial discretion. Section 4405 provides that the court retains jurisdiction to modify or terminate a support order under this Part where justice requires, stating the standard in those general terms rather than by reference to a changed-circumstances test.

THE MISDEMEANOR COUNTERPART — PENAL CODE SECTION 270C
The civil duty has a criminal counterpart. Penal Code section 270c makes it a misdemeanor for an adult child who has the ability to do so to fail to provide necessary food, clothing, shelter, or medical attendance for an indigent parent. The section opens with an express exception for Family Code Chapter 2 of Part 4 of Division 9 — the abandonment-relief chapter described elsewhere in this document — so that an order under that chapter operates against the criminal provision as well as the civil one. The Penal Code section uses the word “indigent,” where the Family Code section uses “in need and unable to self-maintain by work”; the two provisions are not worded identically.

THE PUBLIC-BENEFITS DISPLACEMENT — WELFARE AND INSTITUTIONS CODE SECTION 12350
Section 4400's opening words, “Except as otherwise provided by law,” do real work. Welfare and Institutions Code section 12350, in the article titled “Relatives' Responsibility” within the chapter governing California's State Supplementary Program for the Aged, Blind and Disabled, provides that no relative shall be held legally liable to support or contribute to the support of an applicant for or recipient of aid under that chapter. A second paragraph states that, notwithstanding Family Code sections 3910, 4400, and 4401 and Penal Code section 270c, no demand shall be made upon any relative to support or contribute toward the support of such an applicant or recipient, and forbids a county or its officers from threatening a relative with legal action or any penalty. The naming of sections 4400 and 4401 in that “notwithstanding” clause is the clearest statutory example of the “except as otherwise provided by law” carve-out at work.

HOW A COURT OF APPEAL HAS READ THE PUBLIC-BENEFITS DISPLACEMENT — MARRIAGE OF CADY & GAMICK (2024)
A 2024 Court of Appeal opinion construed Welfare and Institutions Code section 12350 narrowly. The court held that the Legislature intended that section to prevent government actors from seeking reimbursement for the cost of government assistance from relatives of aid recipients, and that because the section bars only the government from seeking contribution, it does not bar a parent from seeking a court order requiring the other parent to contribute to the support of an adult disabled child under Family Code section 3910. The court reached that reading over an argument that the statute's “notwithstanding” clause would be surplusage unless it reached private claims as well.

RELIEF FROM THE DUTY WHEN THE PARENT ABANDONED THE CHILD — FAMILY CODE SECTIONS 4410, 4411, AND 4414
Chapter 2 of the same Part creates a petition procedure by which an adult child may seek an order freeing the petitioner from the obligation to support the parent. Section 4410 fixes venue: the petition is filed in the county where the parent resides, or, if the parent does not reside in California, in the county where the adult child resides. Section 4411 states that the court shall make the order only if the petition alleges and the court finds all three of the following: that the parent abandoned the child while the child was a minor; that the abandonment continued for two or more years before the child turned 18; and that during the period of abandonment the parent was physically and mentally able to provide support. Section 4414 states the effect of a granted petition — the petitioner is relieved of the support obligation and is also released from any state law requiring a child to pay for a parent's support, care, or maintenance, or to reimburse the state or a local public agency for furnishing it.

NOTICE AND TIMING IN AN ABANDONMENT-RELIEF PROCEEDING — FAMILY CODE SECTIONS 4412 AND 4413
Two sections govern process. Section 4412 provides that on the filing of the petition the clerk sets the matter for hearing and issues a citation stating the time and place, directed to the parent and to the parent's conservator if any, or, if the parent is deceased, to the personal representative of the parent's estate; the citation and a copy of the petition must be personally served on each person to whom the citation is directed at least five days before the hearing, in the manner provided for service of summons. Section 4413 adds a jurisdictional waiting period where the parent is a California resident: the court does not have jurisdiction to make an order until 30 days after the county counsel — or the district attorney, in a county without a county counsel — of the county where the parent resides has been served with notice of the pendency of the proceeding.

At least five days before the date of the hearing, the citation and a copy of the petition shall be personally served on each person to whom it is directed, in the same manner as provided by law for the service of summons."

expectedJSON.body: A 2024 Court of Appeal opinion construed Welfare and Institutions Code section 12350 narrowly. The court held that the Legislature intended that section to prevent government actors from seeking reimbursement for the cost of government assistance from relatives of aid recipients, and that because the section bars only the government from seeking contribution, it does not bar a parent from seeking a court order requiring the other parent to contribute to the support of an adult disabled child under Family Code section 3910. The court reached that reading over an argument that the statute's “notwithstanding” clause would be surplusage unless it reached private claims as well.

citations.quote: The Legislature intended Welfare and Institutions Code section 12350 to prevent government actors from seeking reimbursement for the cost of government assistance from relatives of aid recipients.

citations.quote: Because Welfare and Institutions Code section 12350 bars only the government from seeking contribution from relatives to defray the costs of such aid, it does not bar a parent from seeking a court order requiring the other parent to contribute to the support of an adult disabled child under Family Code section 3910.

expectedJSON.body: Chapter 2 of the same Part creates a petition procedure by which an adult child may seek an order freeing the petitioner from the obligation to support the parent. Section 4410 fixes venue: the petition is filed in the county where the parent resides, or, if the parent does not reside in California, in the county where the adult child resides. Section 4411 states that the court shall make the order only if the petition alleges and the court finds all three of the following: that the parent abandoned the child while the child was a minor; that the abandonment continued for two or more years before the child turned 18; and that during the period of abandonment the parent was physically and mentally able to provide support. Section 4414 states the effect of a granted petition — the petitioner is relieved of the support obligation and is also released from any state law requiring a child to pay for a parent's support, care, or maintenance, or to reimburse the state or a local public agency for furnishing it.

citations.cite: who may petition, and where the petition is filed
citations.quote: An adult child may file a petition in the county where a parent of the child resides requesting that the court make an order freeing the petitioner from the obligation otherwise imposed by law to support the parent. If the parent does not reside in this state, the petition shall be filed in the county where the adult child resides.

citations.cite: the three findings required before the order may be made
citations.quote: The court shall make the order requested pursuant to Section 4410 only if the petition alleges and the court finds all of the following: (a) The child was abandoned by the parent when the child was a minor. (b) The abandonment continued for a period of two or more years before the time the child attained the age of 18 years. (c) During the period of abandonment the parent was physically and mentally able to provide support for the child.

citations.cite: the relief granted, and its reach into reimbursement statutes
citations.quote: (a) If, upon hearing, the court determines that the requirements of Section 4411 are satisfied, the court shall make an order that the petitioner is relieved from the obligation otherwise imposed by law to support the parent. (b) An order under this section also releases the petitioner with respect to any state law under which a child is required to do any of the following: (1) Pay for the support, care, maintenance, and the like of a parent. (2) Reimburse the state or a local public agency for furnishing the support, care, maintenance, or the like of a parent.

The statute does not define “abandoned,” and this document does not supply a definition or point to one elsewhere in the Family Code. A negative case-law result is recorded rather than omitted: CourtListener full-text searches for the exact phrases “Family Code section 4411” and “Family Code section 4414” each returned zero opinions on the checked date, so no published decision construing the abandonment findings or the scope of the resulting order was located, and this clause rests on the statutory text alone. expectedJSON.body: Two sections govern process. Section 4412 provides that on the filing of the petition the clerk sets the matter for hearing and issues a citation stating the time and place, directed to the parent and to the parent's conservator if any, or, if the parent is deceased, to the personal representative of the parent's estate; the citation and a copy of the petition must be personally served on each person to whom the citation is directed at least five days before the hearing, in the manner provided for service of summons. Section 4413 adds a jurisdictional waiting period where the parent is a California resident: the court does not have jurisdiction to make an order until 30 days after the county counsel — or the district attorney, in a county without a county counsel — of the county where the parent resides has been served with notice of the pendency of the proceeding.

citations.cite: citation, persons served, and the five-day personal service requirement
citations.quote: On the filing of a petition under this chapter, the clerk shall set the matter for hearing by the court and shall issue a citation, stating the time and place of the hearing, directed to the parent and to the parent’s conservator, if any, or, if the parent is deceased, the personal representative of the parent’s estate. At least five days before the date of the hearing, the citation and a copy of the petition shall be personally served on each person to whom it is directed, in the same manner as provided by law for the service of summons.

citations.cite: the 30-day notice to county counsel as a condition of jurisdiction
citations.quote: If the parent is a resident of this state, the court does not have jurisdiction to make an order under this chapter until 30 days after the county counsel, or the district attorney in a county not having a county counsel, of the county in which the parent resides has been served with notice of the pendency of the proceeding.

expectedJSON.body: A 2006 Court of Appeal decision is the principal modern California authority applying the parent-support duty inside a dissolution. The court observed that, though not commonly known, California is one of many states with filial responsibility laws imposing on adult children support obligations akin to those imposed on parents of minor children. It reversed a trial court ruling that a husband's expenditure of community funds on his ailing mother was an unauthorized gift, reasoning that a statutory obligation is a “debt” for purposes of the community-liability statute, so the support obligation was a community obligation rather than the husband's alone, and payment of a community obligation is not an unauthorized gift. The court further noted that while the Family Code creates a community right of reimbursement where community property satisfies certain child or spousal support obligations, no similar statute applies to payment of support to an indigent parent, and it had been pointed to no other statute imposing a reimbursement obligation. The matter was remanded for the husband to establish that the funds were in fact expended to support a mother who was in need and unable to maintain herself.

citations.cite: California is among the states with filial responsibility laws
citations.quote: Though not commonly known, California is one of many states that have enacted filial responsibility laws imposing on adult children obligations of support akin to those imposed on parents with respect to minor children.

citations.cite: the parent-support obligation as a community, not separate, obligation
citations.quote: Husband’s support obligation, if any existed, was not Husband’s alone. It was a community obligation. It cannot be plausibly argued that payment of a community obligation constitutes an unauthorized gift.

citations.cite: no statute requires reimbursement of the community for support paid to an indigent parent
citations.quote: However, no similar statute applies to payment of support to an indigent parent, and we have been pointed to no other statute imposing a reimbursement obligation.

expectedJSON.gap: The reversal was for further proceedings, not a finding that the duty existed on those facts; the appellate court expressly left the husband to establish on remand that the funds were spent supporting a parent in need. expectedJSON.body: The duty's constitutional footing was litigated in the California Supreme Court in 1973. Adult children of recipients of aid to the aged argued that requiring them to reimburse the state arbitrarily charged the cost of public assistance to one class of citizens. A divided court rejected the challenge under the rational-relationship test, reasoning that selecting adult children is rational because the parents who are now in need supported and cared for those children during their minority, and that a rational basis for the classification is found in, and provided by, Civil Code section 206 — the predecessor of Family Code section 4400 — which the court said rests soundly on the Anglo-American legal tradition. Justice Tobriner dissented, arguing the decision departed from Department of Mental Hygiene v. Kirchner (1964) 60 Cal.2d 716 and its line of cases.

citations.quote: It seems eminently clear that the selection of the adult children is rational on the ground that the parents, who are now in need, supported and cared for their children during their minority and that such children should in return now support their parents to the extent to which they are capable.

citations.cite: former Civil Code section 206 as the rational basis for the classification
citations.quote: A rational basis for such classification is found in, and provided by, Civil Code section 206, which itself rests soundly on our Anglo-American legal tradition.

expectedJSON.body: A 2001 Court of Appeal opinion declined to borrow section 4400 as the yardstick for a different statute. Parents seeking standing to sue for their child's wrongful death as “dependent” parents under Code of Civil Procedure section 377.60 confronted an argument that the support contemplated by Family Code section 4400 is the same support the wrongful death statute requires. The court disagreed, stating that the proper measure of dependence is not found in section 4400. It explained that the main purpose of section 4400 is to keep indigents from becoming public charges, while the purpose behind the wrongful death statute is to compensate tort victims, and that the two statutes envision different support thresholds — section 4400 compelling support for parents who are in need and unable to maintain themselves, while wrongful death standing runs to parents who relied to some extent on a child's financial support for the necessities of life.

citations.quote: But we do not agree with defendant that the proper measure of dependence is found in Family Code section 4400.

citations.cite: the purpose of section 4400 as the court described it
citations.quote: The main purpose of Family Code section 4400 is to keep indigents from becoming public charges.
